Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

SEOUL, South Korea (CNN)  -- South Korea will open its market to most U.S. beef, a senior government official said Thursday, according to state media. Thousands of people have taken to the streets of the South Korean capital in protest at the deal . South Korea banned imports of U.S. beef in 2003 amid concerns over a case of mad cow disease in the United States. The ban closed what was then the third-largest market for U.S. beef exporters. It resumed limited imports last year -- allowing boneless beef from cattle under 30 months of age -- but that re-opening was subject to interruptions and closed altogether in October 2007. A deal that South Korea and the United States struck last month bans the import of high-risk materials, like tonsils, brains, spinal cord marrow and a section of the small intestine, Agriculture Minister Chung Woon-chun said Thursday, according to South Korea's Yonhap news agency. These parts pose the greatest risk of transmitting mad cow disease to humans. The ban will be lifted within a few days, once the government's new import rules have been published. The pending resumption of U.S. beef imports hasn't been without political costs for President Lee Myung-bak. He apologized to the nation last week for failing to fully understand concerns about mad cow disease. In downtown Seoul, thousands of people have regularly staged protests, chanting "We don't want crazy cows," since the deal to revive beef imports was announced. And the main opposition party has taken up the fight. "We will be forced to make a critical decision if the government pushes through its plan to announce resumption of beef imports," said Sohn Hak-kyu, leader of the main opposition United Democratic Party, Yonhap reported. "If the government and the ruling party ignore this warning, we will come up with every possible measure to stop them." The opposition has already filed a suit to suspend implementation of new beef import terms, according to Yonhap. Lee's ruling Grand National Party (GNP) is working to soothe tensions, saying that American beef is safe to eat and that adequate safety precautions have been taken. "The government has tried its best to free the public from unnecessary concerns, and sufficient countermeasures have been prepared," said Lee Hahn-koo, the party's chief policymaker, Yonhap reported. When South Korea and the United States reached the deal in April to re-open the South Korean market, they removed the major obstacle to U.S. congressional approval of the Korea-U.S. Free Trade Agreement (FTA). Lee urged the National Assembly this month to ratify the agreement as soon as possible to provide fresh impetus to the sluggish Korean economy, saying it will create 300,000 jobs. But the opposition has promised to fight the FTA until the beef pact is nullified. In 2003, the United States exported $815 million pounds of beef and beef variety meats to South Korea. The U.S. beef industry has lost up to $4 billion since the market closed, according to the U.S. Meat Export Federation.

SEOUL, South Korea (CNN) — A high-ranking South Korean official announced Thursday that the country plans to allow most American beef back into its market, state media reported. The agreement has triggered demonstrations involving thousands of people in Seoul.

South Korea halted U.S. beef imports in 2003 after a case of mad cow disease was discovered in the United States. At the time, South Korea was the third-biggest overseas market for American beef producers. Limited trade restarted last year, with imports restricted to boneless meat from cattle younger than 30 months. However, shipments were repeatedly disrupted, and the market shut down again entirely in October 2007.

Under an agreement reached by Seoul and Washington last month, imports will exclude materials considered especially dangerous, Agriculture Minister Chung Woon-chun said Thursday, according to South Korea’s Yonhap news agency. Prohibited items include tonsils, brains, spinal cord marrow, and part of the small intestine. These tissues are regarded as carrying the highest risk of passing mad cow disease to people.

The remaining ban is expected to end within days, after the government formally publishes its revised import regulations.

The planned return of U.S. beef has created political difficulties for President Lee Myung-bak. Last week, he apologized publicly for not adequately recognizing the population’s fears about mad cow disease. Since the import agreement was unveiled, thousands of protesters have repeatedly gathered in central Seoul, shouting, “We don’t want crazy cows.”

The country’s largest opposition party has also challenged the policy. Sohn Hak-kyu, head of the main opposition United Democratic Party, warned that his party would have to take a major step if the government proceeded with its announcement reopening the market, Yonhap reported. He said the opposition would use every available means to block the move if the government and governing party disregarded the warning.

Yonhap also reported that the opposition has already brought a lawsuit seeking to halt enforcement of the new beef-import conditions.

Meanwhile, Lee’s governing Grand National Party is attempting to ease public anxiety. It maintains that U.S. beef is safe for consumption and that proper safeguards are in place. Lee Hahn-koo, the GNP’s chief policy official, said the government had done everything possible to address what he called needless public worries and had developed sufficient protective measures, according to Yonhap.

The April agreement to reopen South Korea’s beef market also eliminated the principal barrier to U.S. congressional approval of the Korea-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. This month, Lee called on the National Assembly to ratify the FTA quickly, arguing that it would energize South Korea’s weak economy and generate 300,000 jobs. The opposition, however, has pledged to resist the trade agreement unless the beef deal is canceled.

In 2003, U.S. exports of beef and assorted beef products to South Korea totaled 815 million pounds. According to the U.S. Meat Export Federation, the American beef sector has lost as much as $4 billion since South Korea closed its market.

**South Korea reopens market to most U.S. beef despite protests**

**SEOUL, South Korea** — South Korea reopened its market to most U.S. beef imports Thursday, moving ahead with a deal that has sparked weeks of mass demonstrations over fears of mad cow disease.

Under revised rules, U.S. beef from cattle younger than 30 months can enter the country, while certain materials considered at higher risk of carrying bovine spongiform encephalopathy, or BSE, will remain prohibited. U.S. exporters also agreed to a voluntary age-verification system intended to reassure Korean consumers.

The government says the imports are safe and meet international standards. Officials have argued that the risk of contracting the human form of BSE from American beef is extremely low.

But the assurances have failed to calm many South Koreans. Tens of thousands of protesters have filled central Seoul in candlelight demonstrations, accusing the government of moving too quickly and failing to secure adequate safeguards.

The dispute has become a major political crisis for President Lee Myung-bak, whose approval ratings plunged amid criticism of the agreement. Lee apologized for not listening closely enough to public concerns and replaced several senior aides.

South Korea suspended U.S. beef imports in 2003 after the first American case of mad cow disease was confirmed. Before the ban, the country was one of the largest overseas markets for U.S. beef.

Washington welcomed the reopening, saying American beef is safe. However, opposition lawmakers and civic groups in South Korea vowed to continue pressing the government for stricter controls.

BSE damages the brain and nervous system of cattle. In rare cases, people who consume contaminated tissue can develop variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, a fatal neurological illness.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed news article explaining the 2008 U.S.–South Korea beef import agreement, the public backlash in Seoul, and its connection to the Korea-U.S. Free Trade Agreement.
counterfactuals.output:
# How a Beef Deal With Washington Ignited Mass Protests in Seoul—and Became Entangled With a Free-Trade Pact

**SEOUL —** An agreement intended to remove a major obstacle in U.S.–South Korean trade relations instead became one of the defining political crises of South Korean President Lee Myung-bak’s first year in office.

The April 2008 beef import accord reopened South Korea’s market broadly to American beef after years of restrictions imposed over bovine spongiform encephalopathy, commonly known as mad cow disease. Washington viewed the agreement as a science-based normalization of trade. Many South Koreans saw it as a hastily negotiated concession that exposed consumers to unnecessary risk and was made to advance a larger free-trade agenda.

The resulting candlelight demonstrations drew tens of thousands of people into central Seoul, damaged Lee’s approval ratings, forced his government to reshuffle senior officials and led the two countries to add safeguards limiting the beef shipped to South Korea.

The dispute was closely connected to the Korea-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, or KORUS FTA. The beef agreement and the trade pact were legally separate, but U.S. lawmakers and agricultural interests treated restored access for American beef as an important political condition for moving the broader accord forward.

## A market closed after the first U.S. mad cow case

South Korea had been one of the largest foreign markets for American beef. That trade stopped in December 2003, when the United States reported its first confirmed case of bovine spongiform encephalopathy, or BSE, in a cow in Washington state that had been imported from Canada.

BSE is a fatal neurological disease in cattle caused by abnormal proteins known as prions. In rare circumstances, people who consume contaminated tissue can develop variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. The highest-risk tissues—known as specified risk materials—include parts of the brain, skull, spinal cord and certain sections of the intestine, with the exact regulatory definition depending partly on an animal’s age.

South Korea, like many U.S. trading partners, suspended American beef imports after the 2003 case. The countries later negotiated a limited reopening. In 2006, Seoul agreed to accept boneless beef from cattle younger than 30 months, an age threshold used because BSE risk rises in older animals.

That partial arrangement remained unstable. South Korean inspectors repeatedly found prohibited bone fragments or other material in shipments, prompting suspensions, rejections and further negotiations.

From Washington’s perspective, the restrictions were excessive. The World Organisation for Animal Health, then commonly known by its French abbreviation OIE, classified the United States in 2007 as a country with “controlled risk” for BSE. U.S. officials argued that this status supported broader market access if specified risk materials were removed and other safeguards were followed.

South Korean critics countered that an international risk classification did not require Seoul to abandon its own age-based restrictions or accept every U.S. processing practice.

## The April 2008 agreement

On April 18, 2008, shortly before Lee met President George W. Bush at Camp David, U.S. and South Korean negotiators announced a new import protocol.

The agreement sharply expanded the range of American beef eligible for sale in South Korea. It permitted bone-in cuts, including ribs, and created a path for imports from cattle aged 30 months or older. The opening was to proceed in stages, tied in part to U.S. implementation of strengthened animal-feed controls.

The protocol also set rules for excluding specified risk materials. For cattle younger than 30 months, certain tissues were prohibited; for older cattle, the list was broader. U.S. processing plants exporting to South Korea were required to operate under inspection and certification systems intended to keep barred tissues out of shipments.

To trade officials, these were technical provisions based on international standards. To many South Koreans, however, the headline was simpler: the government had agreed to accept beef from older American cattle after previously insisting on a younger-than-30-month limit.

The timing compounded the controversy. Lee had taken office in February promising closer ties with Washington and a business-friendly economic program. His critics alleged that he had relaxed food-safety standards to produce an early diplomatic success before his summit with Bush.

The government denied sacrificing public health, saying U.S. beef was safe and that the agreement reflected scientific evidence and internationally recognized risk controls.

## Candlelight protests and an explosion of public distrust

The first candlelight vigil against the agreement took place in Seoul on May 2. What began as a protest heavily attended by teenagers and young internet users grew into weeks of mass demonstrations involving parents, labor unions, civic groups, opposition parties, religious organizations and people angry about a broader range of Lee administration policies.

At their height, the protests filled streets around Seoul City Hall and the central government district. Police erected barricades, and some late-night demonstrations ended in clashes, injuries and mass detentions. Water cannons were used against protesters, creating images that further intensified public anger.

The movement was fueled by television reports, online forums and social media platforms that were becoming increasingly influential in South Korean politics. Claims circulated that Koreans were unusually susceptible to variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, that American beef could enter school lunches without meaningful controls, and that the government would be unable to stop unsafe shipments.

Some of the most alarming assertions were exaggerated, misleading or scientifically unsupported. A controversial episode of the television investigative program **“PD Notebook”** amplified fears with a report about BSE and the U.S. cattle industry; portions of its presentation and translation were later challenged.

But the scale of the demonstrations could not be explained by misinformation alone. The deeper issue was trust.

Critics said the Lee government had negotiated without adequate transparency, failed to communicate the technical details and appeared dismissive when the public raised concerns. Consumers also questioned whether South Korea retained enough power under the protocol to halt imports immediately if another BSE case emerged.

The beef issue became a vehicle for wider dissatisfaction with Lee’s governing style. His administration was viewed by opponents as overly deferential to Washington, insufficiently consultative at home and too eager to push through market-oriented reforms.

Lee apologized to the public, and his entire cabinet offered to resign amid the crisis. Several senior officials were eventually replaced. His approval rating, already under pressure, fell sharply.

## A supplemental arrangement limits imports by age

Unable to calm the protests through public assurances alone, Seoul returned to Washington seeking additional protections.

In June 2008, the two sides announced what South Korean officials called additional or supplemental arrangements. Rather than formally rewriting the entire April protocol, the compromise relied heavily on a voluntary commercial restriction backed by a U.S. government verification system.

Under the arrangement, U.S. exporters participating in trade with South Korea would ship beef only from cattle younger than 30 months. The U.S. Department of Agriculture established a Quality System Assessment program to verify compliance, and South Korean importers agreed not to purchase beef from older animals.

The compromise also strengthened labeling, inspection and auditing provisions and clarified procedures for handling food-safety concerns. South Korean authorities were given additional opportunities to inspect U.S. facilities and reject shipments that did not meet the agreed conditions.

The under-30-month restriction was technically described as voluntary because it rested on industry participation rather than a permanent U.S. legal ban. In practical terms, however, it became a condition for access to the South Korean market and addressed the public’s central demand.

American beef sales resumed, and the protests gradually subsided, though distrust of the Lee administration persisted.

## The link to the Korea-U.S. Free Trade Agreement

The beef controversy cannot be understood without the KORUS FTA.

The United States and South Korea had signed the free-trade agreement on June 30, 2007, during the administrations of Bush and South Korean President Roh Moo-hyun. It was the largest U.S. trade agreement since the North American Free Trade Agreement and was designed to reduce barriers across a wide range of sectors, including automobiles, financial services, pharmaceuticals, agriculture and industrial goods.

For U.S. cattle producers, South Korea’s market was especially valuable. Before the 2003 ban, South Korea had been among the top destinations for U.S. beef, favored in part for dishes such as grilled short ribs.

The KORUS pact itself addressed tariffs and market access over the long term. South Korea’s 40 percent tariff on U.S. beef was scheduled to be eliminated gradually over 15 years, with a temporary agricultural safeguard available if imports surged.

But the FTA did not by itself settle the post-BSE health restrictions. Those rules were handled through a separate sanitary and veterinary negotiation.

That legal distinction did not prevent the issues from becoming politically intertwined.

Members of Congress from cattle-producing states, as well as U.S. farm groups, argued that lawmakers should not approve a comprehensive trade agreement with South Korea while Seoul continued to restrict American beef. The Bush administration therefore regarded a satisfactory beef protocol as essential to building congressional support for KORUS.

Lee also had strong reasons to resolve the dispute. He supported the trade pact as part of a strategy to deepen the alliance with the United States and make South Korea more competitive. The April 2008 beef agreement was widely seen as an attempt to clear a major political roadblock before his summit with Bush.

That perception drove much of the backlash. To opponents, the government appeared to have put ratification of the FTA—and Lee’s relationship with Washington—ahead of consumer safety. Officials insisted the beef rules were scientifically justified and that no political trade-off had been made.

The most accurate description is that the two agreements were **formally separate but politically connected**. The beef protocol was not a chapter added to KORUS, nor was the free-trade pact automatically ratified once beef imports resumed. Yet without restored beef access, the FTA faced even stronger resistance in the U.S. Congress.

## Ratification came years later

Solving the beef dispute did not produce immediate approval of the trade pact.

When President Barack Obama took office in 2009, his administration sought additional changes, particularly in the automotive sector. Washington and Seoul reached a supplemental trade agreement in December 2010 that adjusted automobile provisions and some tariff schedules.

The U.S. Congress approved KORUS in October 2011. South Korea’s National Assembly ratified it the following month amid another bitter political confrontation, including opposition claims that the agreement favored large corporations and constrained public regulation.

The pact entered into force on March 15, 2012.

By then, U.S. beef had reestablished itself in South Korea. Consumer resistance diminished as imports continued without a major public-health incident, and South Korea again became one of the most important overseas markets for American beef.

## A dispute about more than food safety

The 2008 crisis left a lasting mark on South Korean politics. It demonstrated the mobilizing power of online networks and candlelight protests, a form of civic action that would reappear in later national movements. It also showed how technical trade negotiations can become explosive when they touch food, health, sovereignty and trust in government.

For Washington, the dispute highlighted the domestic political importance of agricultural market access. For Seoul, it revealed the danger of treating a scientifically complex agreement as a narrow regulatory matter while underestimating public concern over transparency and national autonomy.

The final compromise did not amount to a finding that U.S. beef was broadly unsafe. Nor did the protests simply result from irrational fear. The crisis grew from a combination of genuine anxiety about BSE, sensational claims, poor government communication, distrust of the Lee administration and suspicion that the broader free-trade relationship had dictated the outcome.

In that sense, the 2008 beef agreement became far more than an import protocol. It was a test of how two allies balanced science, commerce and democratic consent—and of how a single unresolved agricultural dispute could threaten a trade pact spanning much of their economic relationship.

## South Korea agrees to reopen market to U.S. beef

**SEOUL, April 18, 2008** — South Korea agreed to lift most restrictions on imports of American beef, ending a trade dispute that began after the United States reported its first case of bovine spongiform encephalopathy, or mad-cow disease, in December 2003.

Under the agreement, South Korea would initially permit bone-in and boneless beef from cattle younger than 30 months. Once the United States implemented tighter animal-feed controls, imports from older cattle would also be allowed. The deal removed a significant obstacle ahead of President Lee Myung-bak’s meeting with U.S. President George W. Bush and improved prospects for ratification of the Korea-U.S. free-trade agreement.

South Korean Agriculture Minister Chung Woon-chun said the government had secured safeguards to protect consumers. “The safety of the people was our top priority in the negotiations,” he said, adding that imports could be stopped if a serious health risk emerged.

U.S. Trade Representative Susan Schwab welcomed the agreement, calling it “a win for American ranchers and Korean consumers.” The deal, she said, restored access to what had once been one of the most important overseas markets for U.S. beef.

Opposition politicians accused Lee’s government of making concessions to Washington for political reasons. Democratic Party officials described the agreement as “humiliating diplomacy,” while party leader Sohn Hak-kyu said the government had surrendered South Korea’s “quarantine sovereignty” by accepting beef from older animals.

### Background of the ban

South Korea imposed a complete ban on U.S. beef in December 2003 after a cow in Washington state tested positive for BSE. Before the ban, South Korea was the third-largest foreign market for American beef, buying roughly **$800 million to $850 million** worth in 2003.

Seoul partially reopened the market in 2006, but only to boneless meat from cattle under 30 months. Shipments were repeatedly rejected or suspended after inspectors found bone fragments and other material prohibited under the rules then in force.

### Cost to American exporters

The closure sharply reduced sales for U.S. cattle producers, meatpackers and exporters. Losing a market worth more than $800 million annually deprived the industry of several billion dollars in potential trade during the ban. Industry groups said a fully reopened South Korean market could eventually generate **more than $1 billion a year** in U.S. beef exports.

The decision nevertheless remained politically volatile in South Korea. Public concern about food safety soon fueled large demonstrations, and the two governments later negotiated additional arrangements under which major U.S. suppliers would export only beef from cattle younger than 30 months until Korean consumers regained confidence.

Under the import agreement, South Korea would initially accept bone-in and boneless beef from U.S. cattle younger than 30 months. Beef from older cattle could eventually be permitted after the United States strengthened its animal-feed rules, although specified risk materials linked to bovine spongiform encephalopathy, or mad cow disease, would remain prohibited.

Those banned materials include tonsils and the end of the small intestine from cattle of any age, as well as brains, eyes, skulls, spinal cords and most of the vertebral column from cattle 30 months or older.

Protesters say the safeguards are inadequate and accuse Lee’s government of moving too quickly to satisfy Washington. The demonstrations, which began with students and civic groups, have broadened into a wider expression of anger over Lee’s leadership.

Lee apologized for failing to address public concerns and said his government would not allow imports of beef from cattle older than 30 months unless South Koreans accepted them. His administration also sought additional assurances and voluntary export restrictions from the United States.

Opposition lawmakers, meanwhile, pressed for the agreement to be renegotiated and pursued legislation that would tighten quarantine standards or prevent the government from implementing the deal. They also threatened broader parliamentary action, including moves against cabinet officials responsible for the negotiations.

The dispute has strained Lee’s government only months after he took office and complicated Seoul’s efforts to strengthen economic and diplomatic ties with Washington.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the political and economic controversy surrounding South Korea’s reopening to U.S. beef after mad cow disease fears, using the tone and structure of an international cable news article.
counterfactuals.output:
**Seoul, South Korea —** South Korea’s decision to reopen its market to U.S. beef triggered one of the country’s most serious political crises in years, pitting public-health fears and national pride against trade interests and Seoul’s alliance with Washington.

The dispute erupted in 2008 after President Lee Myung-bak’s government agreed to resume broad imports of American beef. South Korea had restricted the trade following the 2003 discovery of bovine spongiform encephalopathy, commonly known as mad cow disease, in the United States.

The agreement was economically significant. Washington viewed restored access to what had once been a major market for U.S. beef as an important trade objective and as a step toward advancing the Korea-U.S. free-trade agreement. Seoul argued that reopening would strengthen commercial ties, reduce consumer prices and remove a major obstacle in relations with its key ally.

But many South Koreans believed the government had moved too quickly and accepted inadequate safeguards. Television reports and online claims—some later criticized as exaggerated or inaccurate—intensified fears that imported beef could expose consumers to the fatal human form of the disease. Particular concern focused on the age of cattle and the removal of specified risk materials.

The backlash grew into weeks of candlelight demonstrations in central Seoul, drawing students, families, labor groups and opposition activists. Although the protests began over food safety, they broadened into a wider challenge to Lee’s leadership, including accusations that he had placed U.S. interests above public opinion and failed to consult citizens transparently.

Lee apologized and reshuffled senior officials as his approval ratings plunged. His government also sought additional assurances from Washington, including arrangements intended to limit imports from older cattle and strengthen inspection and labeling measures.

Supporters of the deal said the scientific risk was extremely low and accused opposition groups of exploiting public anxiety. Critics countered that the controversy was as much about democratic accountability and sovereignty as it was about epidemiology.

The crisis underscored the political cost of linking sensitive consumer-safety issues to major trade negotiations. While U.S. beef eventually returned to South Korean shelves and regained a substantial share of the market, the episode left lasting scars on Lee’s presidency and became a defining example of how public mistrust can transform a technical trade decision into a national political confrontation.
